title: Assess AI Data and Model Supply Chain Risks
intro: The technical side of AI supply chain risk: assessing third-party, open and public datasets before they shape your models; verifying the provenance and authenticity of the models, data and components vendors supply; and managing the risks you inherit when you build on foundation and pre-trained models.
objectives: Assess third-party, open and public datasets for poisoning, rights, personal data, harmful content, bias and provenance, and apply controls such as hash pinning and internal mirrors
Verify the provenance and authenticity of vendor-supplied models, datasets and components, and defend against typosquatting, namespace reuse and dependency confusion
Identify the risks inherited from foundation and pre-trained models, and manage them through selection, evaluation, safe operation, re-testing and exit planning

sections.title: Assessing third-party, open and public datasets

blocks.title: Where did this data come from?

scenes.title: Where did this data come from?
scenes.sub: Risk assessment for third-party, open and public datasets
scenes.say: Most AI systems are built on data that someone else collected: open datasets, web crawls, purchased data and vendor-labelled examples. | This video covers how to assess the supply chain risk of datasets you don’t control, before they shape your models.

scenes.title: Where AI training data comes from
scenes.say: Training data arrives through many channels. | Web crawls are huge, unvetted and constantly changing. | Open datasets come from model hubs, research groups and benchmark collections. | Purchased data comes from brokers and specialist vendors. | Labels often come from crowdsourcing platforms or outsourced labelling firms. | Synthetic data is generated by other models, and inherits their flaws. | And partner data is shared under agreements whose terms limit how it can be used.

scenes.title: What can go wrong

items.d: No record of origin or changes

scenes.say: Six kinds of risk recur. | Poisoning: samples planted or manipulated to change model behaviour. | Licence and copyright terms that don’t allow your intended use. | Personal data collected without a lawful basis for training. | Illegal or harmful content, which creates legal liability and reputational harm. | Bias, gaps and mislabelling that make the data unrepresentative. | And unknown provenance: no reliable record of where the data came from or how it has changed.

scenes.title: Why URL-based datasets can be poisoned
scenes.say: Poisoning large public datasets is more practical than it sounds. Many web-scale datasets are distributed as lists of web addresses, and each user fetches the content later. | Over time, some of the domains in those lists expire. | In 2023, researchers showed that an attacker could register expired domains and serve new content from them, gaining control of a small share of a major dataset for around sixty dollars. | Anyone who downloaded the dataset afterwards would silently receive the attacker’s content. A related route is editing sources such as Wikipedia just before a scheduled snapshot. | The defence is simple and effective: record a cryptographic hash of every item when the dataset is curated, and reject anything that no longer matches.

scenes.title: A dataset risk assessment
scenes.say: A repeatable assessment has six steps. First, inventory the source: who owns it, what it will be used for, and how critical it is. | Second, establish provenance and rights: where the data came from, under what licence, and with what consent or lawful basis. | Third, inspect the content itself for personal data, secrets, illegal material, duplicates, outliers and signs of poisoning. | Fourth, apply controls: pin the exact version by hash, keep an internal mirror, and filter or remove what fails inspection. | Fifth, document the result in a datasheet and the risk record, and get approval in proportion to the risk. | And sixth, review it periodically, and whenever the source is updated or an advisory is published.

items: Know every external data source and its use
Assess poisoning, rights, personal data, content, bias, provenance
Pin by hash and mirror internally; never pull live at training time
Document, approve and re-review on updates
scenes.say: To recap. | Know every external data source, and what each one is used for. | Assess it for poisoning, rights, personal data, harmful content, bias and provenance. | Pin datasets by hash and mirror them internally, rather than pulling them live at training time. | And document, approve and review them again whenever they change.

blocks.md:
### Why datasets are a supply chain
A model learns whatever its data contains, so every external dataset is a supplier of behaviour. Unlike software, data can’t easily be "patched" once a model has been trained on it: fixing a problem may mean filtering and retraining (Module 3.3) or unlearning (Module 4.3). The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) lists **LLM03: Supply Chain** and **LLM04: Data and Model Poisoning**, and MITRE ATLAS catalogues techniques such as publishing poisoned datasets.

### Risk factors by source
| Source | Typical risks | Key questions |
|---|---|---|
| **Web crawls** | Poisoning, copyrighted and personal data, illegal content, spam | Is content stored, or only URLs? How was it filtered? Can items be verified by hash? |
| **Open datasets** | Unclear licences, undocumented changes, malicious loading scripts on hubs | Who maintains it? Is there a datasheet? Which version and hash? |
| **Purchased data** | Unlawful collection, resale restrictions, inaccurate records | How was it collected, and with what consent? What do the warranties cover? |
| **Labelling vendors** | Label noise, deliberate mislabelling, data exposure to labellers | How is quality checked? Who sees the data, and where? |
| **Synthetic data** | Inherited bias and errors, licence terms of the generating model, model collapse | Which model generated it, under what terms? How was it validated? |
| **Partner data** | Purpose limits, onward-sharing restrictions, regulatory contamination | What does the agreement allow? Does it carry regulated data (Module 2.4)? |

### Real-world lessons
- **Practical poisoning:** in 2023, Carlini and colleagues showed that poisoning web-scale datasets is practical. Because datasets such as LAION-400M are distributed as URL lists, buying expired domains (*split-view poisoning*) would have let an attacker control about 0.01% of a dataset for around 60 US dollars, and timed edits to Wikipedia before snapshots (*frontrunning*) offered another route. Integrity hashes recorded at curation time defeat split-view poisoning.
- **Illegal content:** in December 2023, researchers found illegal abuse imagery in the LAION-5B image dataset, which was withdrawn and later re-released after cleaning. Anyone who had trained on it faced questions about their models and obligations.
- **Unlawful personal data:** regulators have fined organisations for building facial recognition databases from scraped images without a lawful basis.

### Assessment and controls
1. **Inventory** every external source in the data catalogue and AIBOM, with owner, intended use and criticality (Modules 2.5 and 3.1).
2. **Provenance and rights:** origin, collection method, licence, consent or lawful basis, and any restrictions on derivatives. Tools such as the Data Provenance Initiative’s explorer help trace licences for popular datasets.
3. **Technical inspection:** scan for personal data, secrets, malware and illegal content; deduplicate; profile distributions and labels; look for outliers, near-duplicate clusters and trigger-like patterns that may indicate poisoning.
4. **Controls:** pin versions by **content hash**, keep an **internal mirror** rather than downloading at training time, quarantine new data until it passes checks, disable remote code in dataset loaders, and filter or remove failing items.
5. **Document and approve:** datasheets for datasets, and risk acceptance by the data owner in proportion to the risk.
6. **Monitor:** watch for upstream updates, takedowns, licence changes and security advisories, and re-assess when they occur.

Relevant guidance includes the NIST AI RMF (managing third-party data and model risks), NIST SP 800-161 on supply chain risk management, ISO/IEC 5259 on data quality for machine learning, and ISO/IEC 42001’s Annex A controls on data provenance and quality.

blocks.title: Dataset supply chain questions
blocks.md: Favour answers that **verify and pin** data (hashes, internal mirrors, quarantine) and that **assess rights and provenance before use**. "It’s public, so it’s safe to use" is never the best answer: public data can be poisoned, unlicensed, unlawful or harmful.

blocks.title: Name the dataset risk
pairs: Images are fetched from web addresses that have since changed hands
A data broker can’t say how consent was obtained for its consumer profiles
An open dataset’s licence forbids commercial use
Synthetic training data repeats the generating model’s stereotypes
A labelling contractor deliberately mislabels a small set of examples

q.q: A team’s training pipeline downloads a popular open image dataset directly from its list of source URLs each time a model is retrained. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Keep downloading live, because the newest version of each image is always the most accurate
Verify each item against hashes recorded at curation time, and train from a pinned internal mirror
Switch to a larger open dataset, because more data dilutes any poisoned samples it may contain
Ask the dataset maintainers to confirm by email that none of the URLs have changed since publication
q.why: Live URL downloads let anyone who controls a domain change what you train on. Hash verification and a pinned internal mirror make training data fixed and checkable. Bigger datasets don’t prevent poisoning, and an email confirmation isn’t a control.

sections.title: Verifying provenance and authenticity from vendors

scenes.title: Trust, but verify the artefact
scenes.sub: Provenance and authenticity for models, data and components
scenes.say: Due diligence tells you whether a vendor is trustworthy. Verification tells you whether the specific file in front of you really came from that vendor, unaltered. | This video covers how to verify the provenance and authenticity of models, datasets and software you receive from third parties.

scenes.title: Provenance and authenticity
rows: Where did it come from, and how was it made?
Is it really from who it claims, unaltered?
Keys, accounts or names are hijacked
scenes.say: Two related questions. | Provenance asks where an artefact came from and how it was made. Authenticity asks whether it really comes from who it claims to, unaltered. | Provenance evidence includes build attestations, AI bills of materials and lineage records. Authenticity evidence includes digital signatures, verified publisher accounts and published hashes. | Provenance fails when records are missing or can’t be checked. Authenticity fails when signing keys, publisher accounts or familiar names are taken over by someone else.

scenes.title: How impostors get in
scenes.say: Impostor artefacts get in through familiar routes. | Typosquatting: look-alike names for models and packages. | Namespace reuse: when a publisher deletes or renames an account on a model hub, someone else may register the old name, and pipelines that refer to models by name start pulling the impostor. Researchers demonstrated this against major cloud model catalogues in 2025. | Dependency confusion, where a public package with the same name as an internal one gets installed instead. In December 2022, a malicious package was pulled into PyTorch’s nightly builds this way. | Hijacked publisher accounts and stolen upload tokens. | Altered copies on unofficial mirrors. | And model cards or vendor claims that overstate how a model was tested.

scenes.title: A verification workflow
scenes.say: A verification workflow brings these checks together. Start from the official source, and confirm the publisher’s identity. | Verify the digital signature, and the hash of every file. | Check the provenance evidence: build attestations, the AI bill of materials and the model card. | Scan and test the artefact in a sandbox, converting models to safe formats, and run your own evaluations rather than relying on the vendor’s claims. | Register the approved artefact, and pin it by hash rather than by name, so a renamed or hijacked source can’t substitute something else. | And monitor for security advisories, revoked signatures and takedowns.

items: Provenance: where from and how made; authenticity: really from them, unaltered
Watch for typosquatting, namespace reuse and dependency confusion
Verify signatures, attestations and AIBOMs; test in a sandbox
Pin by hash in an internal registry; monitor for advisories
scenes.say: To recap. | Provenance tells you where an artefact came from and how it was made; authenticity tells you it really came from the claimed source, unaltered. | Watch for typosquatting, namespace reuse, dependency confusion and hijacked accounts. | Verify signatures, attestations and bills of materials, and test artefacts yourself in a sandbox. | And pin approved artefacts by hash in an internal registry, while monitoring for advisories.

blocks.md:
### From vendor trust to artefact trust
Module 2.5 covers **vendor** due diligence: security controls, contracts, SLAs and notification rights. This section covers **artefact** verification: checking each model, dataset, library or container you actually receive. A trustworthy vendor can still be impersonated, compromised or mistaken.

### Evidence you can ask for and check
| Evidence | What it shows | How to check |
|---|---|---|
| **Digital signature** | The artefact was signed by the publisher’s key or verified identity and hasn’t changed | Verify against the publisher’s known key, or a Sigstore certificate tied to their identity and recorded in a transparency log (OpenSSF Model Signing) |
| **Published hashes** | The bytes match what the publisher released | Compare digests obtained through a separate trusted channel |
| **Provenance attestation** | How and where it was built: source, inputs, pipeline (SLSA, in-toto) | Verify the attestation’s signature and check that it matches the artefact’s digest |
| **AIBOM or SBOM** | Components: base model, datasets, libraries, licences (CycloneDX, SPDX) | Cross-check with your inventory; scan listed components for known vulnerabilities |
| **Model card and datasheet** | Intended use, training data, evaluation results, limitations | Compare claims against your own testing |
| **Third-party assurance** | Independent assessment, such as ISO/IEC 42001 certification or SOC 2 reports | Check scope, date and the certifying body |

### Threats to authenticity
- **Typosquatting and look-alike names** on model hubs and package registries.
- **Model namespace reuse:** when a hub account is deleted or transferred, its old name may be re-registered. In 2025, researchers showed that pipelines and cloud model catalogues that referenced models by name could be made to pull attacker-controlled models this way.
- **Dependency confusion:** a public package outranks a private one with the same name. In December 2022, a malicious package named *torchtriton*, uploaded to the public Python package index, was installed by PyTorch’s nightly builds and collected data from affected systems.
- **Compromised publisher accounts and CI pipelines**, which can push signed but malicious releases. Signatures prove who signed, not that the content is safe.
- **Unofficial mirrors and re-uploads** of popular models, sometimes with altered weights or loading code.

### Verification practices
- Download only from **official sources and verified publishers**; prefer hubs and catalogues that show verification status.
- **Pin by immutable identifier**, such as a commit hash or content digest, not by a name or "latest" tag.
- **Verify signatures and hashes** automatically in the pipeline, and fail closed when verification fails.
- **Scan** for unsafe serialisation, embedded code and malware; disable remote code execution in model and dataset loaders; convert to safe formats (Module 3.6).
- **Test** behaviour yourself: capability, safety, bias and security evaluations, including checks for hidden triggers where tools allow.
- **Mirror** approved artefacts in an internal registry, so builds don’t depend on external availability or a name staying in the same hands.
- Use **private package indexes** with scoped names, and configure installers so internal names can’t be satisfied from public registries.
- **Monitor** advisories, revocations, takedowns and changes of ownership for everything in your AIBOM.

blocks.title: Signed is not the same as safe
blocks.md: A valid signature proves **who** signed an artefact and that it **hasn’t changed**. It doesn’t prove the content is free of backdoors or vulnerabilities, because a compromised publisher can sign malicious releases. The best answers combine **verification** (signatures, hashes, provenance) with **independent testing** and **pinning**.

blocks.title: Verification evidence
cards: Shows who signed an artefact and that it hasn’t changed. It doesn’t show the content is safe.
Lets you confirm the bytes match the release, if you obtain the hash through a separate trusted channel.
Signed record of how an artefact was built: source, inputs and pipeline.
Lists the components inside: base model, datasets, libraries and licences.
Independent certification or audit reports. Check their scope and date.

q.q: A production pipeline loads a model from a public hub using only the publisher’s account name and model name. The publisher has just deleted its account. What is the MAIN risk?
o: The model will run more slowly, because the hub no longer caches it near the pipeline
Someone could register the old name and serve a malicious model that the pipeline then loads
The model’s licence automatically becomes void at the moment the publisher deletes its account
The pipeline’s own API keys for the hub will expire at the same moment as the account
q.why: Name-based references trust whoever controls the name. Pinning by content hash or commit and mirroring approved models internally stop a re-registered namespace from substituting a malicious model.

sections.title: Risks of foundation and pre-trained models

blocks.title: What you inherit from a foundation model

scenes.title: What you inherit from a foundation model
scenes.sub: Risks of foundation and pre-trained models
scenes.say: Few organisations train large models from scratch. They start from a foundation model, and inherit everything that came with it: the good, the flawed and the hidden. | This video covers the risks of building on foundation and pre-trained models, and how to manage them.

scenes.title: What a foundation model passes on

layers.label: Hidden behaviours
layers.sub: Backdoors and triggers that survive fine-tuning

layers.label: Fragile safeguards
layers.sub: Safety training that fine-tuning can undo

scenes.say: A foundation model passes on five kinds of risk. | Its training data is largely unknown to you, and may include copyrighted works, personal data, poisoned content and biased samples. | It may carry hidden behaviours, such as backdoors with triggers that survive your fine-tuning. | Its safety training can be fragile: research has shown that fine-tuning, even on a small number of examples, can undo it. | Its licence may restrict how you use it, and pass obligations on to your customers. | And if it is hosted, you depend on the provider for updates, version availability and uptime, which risks lock-in.

scenes.title: Fine-tuning can erode safety training
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative refusal rate on harmful requests, by number of fine-tuning examples
scenes.say: Here is why fine-tuning needs its own safety testing. In this illustrative chart, a model that refused almost all harmful requests is fine-tuned on a small number of harmful examples, and its refusals collapse. Researchers showed in 2023 that around ten such examples could be enough. | Even fine-tuning on ordinary, benign task data can gradually weaken safety behaviour. | So treat every fine-tuned model as a new model: re-run safety and security evaluations before it is approved.

scenes.title: Open weights and hosted APIs
scenes.say: Your risks depend on how you consume the model. | With open weights, you control the weights, the hosting and when you update. With a hosted API, you control only your prompts and integration. | Open weights bring risks such as backdoors, unsafe file formats and licence terms. Hosted models bring silent behaviour changes, outages and questions about how your data is used. | So for open weights: verify, scan, evaluate and pin. For hosted APIs: pin versions, secure the contract and plan fallbacks.

scenes.title: Managing foundation model risk
scenes.say: Five practices manage most of this risk. | Select models deliberately, considering provenance, documentation, licence terms and the provider’s security track record. | Evaluate the model for your own use case: capability, safety, bias and security, not just public benchmark scores. | Load and run it safely: safe file formats, sandboxed environments and least privilege for anything it can call. | Re-test after every fine-tune and every version change. | And plan an exit: an abstraction layer and pre-approved alternatives, so a deprecation, licence change or outage doesn’t strand you.

items: You inherit unknown data, hidden behaviours and licence terms
Fine-tuning can undo safety training: re-test every change
Open weights: verify, scan, pin; hosted: pin, contract, fallback
Select deliberately, evaluate for your use, plan an exit
scenes.say: To recap. | Building on a foundation model means inheriting unknown training data, possible hidden behaviours and licence terms. | Fine-tuning can undo safety training, so re-test every fine-tuned model and every version change. | For open weights, verify, scan and pin. For hosted APIs, pin versions, secure the contract and plan fallbacks. | And select models deliberately, evaluate them for your own use, and always have an exit plan.

blocks.md:
### Inherited risks in detail
| Risk | What it means | Example controls |
|---|---|---|
| **Unknown training data** | Possible copyrighted works, personal data, poisoned or biased content, and benchmark contamination that inflates scores | Provider documentation and training data summaries; your own evaluations; legal review; indemnities where available (Module 2.4) |
| **Backdoors and hidden triggers** | Behaviour that activates only on specific inputs. Anthropic’s 2024 *Sleeper Agents* research showed that deliberately trained backdoors could persist through standard safety training | Trusted sources, provenance checks, behavioural testing, monitoring in production; accept that testing can’t prove absence |
| **Unsafe artefacts** | Pickle-based files that run code on load; malicious loading code | Safe formats, scanning, sandboxed loading, remote code disabled (Module 3.6) |
| **Fragile safety alignment** | Qi and colleagues (2023) showed that fine-tuning on as few as 10 harmful examples could largely remove a model’s safety behaviour, and benign fine-tuning could also degrade it | Re-run safety evaluations after every fine-tune; control who can fine-tune and on what data |
| **Inherited vulnerabilities** | Jailbreaks and adversarial inputs that work on the base model often transfer to its derivatives | Track advisories for the base model; test derivatives against known attacks |
| **Licence restrictions** | Acceptable use policies, user thresholds, field-of-use limits, attribution and pass-through obligations | Licence review before adoption; record licences in the AIBOM |
| **Provider dependence** | Silent updates behind aliases, deprecations, outages, changes to terms or data use | Version pinning, contractual notice periods, fallbacks, exit plans (Modules 2.5 and 3.6) |
| **Concentration risk** | Many organisations relying on a few models, so one flaw or outage spreads widely | Diversity where critical; business continuity planning (Module 5.7) |

### Regulatory context
Under the EU AI Act, providers of **general-purpose AI models** must keep technical documentation, give downstream providers the information they need to understand the model’s capabilities and limitations, have a copyright policy, and publish a summary of training content (Article 53). Providers of models with **systemic risk** have further duties, including model evaluation, adversarial testing, incident reporting and cybersecurity protection (Article 55). If you build a high-risk system on a general-purpose model, you remain responsible for that system’s compliance, so ask for, and use, the provider’s documentation.

### A foundation model adoption checklist
1. **Need and alternatives:** is a foundation model necessary, and which options exist?
2. **Source and provenance:** official publisher, signatures, model card, training data summary, AIBOM.
3. **Licence and terms:** permitted uses, restrictions, data use by hosted providers, indemnities.
4. **Security review:** file formats, loading code, dependencies, hosting architecture, data flows.
5. **Evaluation:** task performance, safety, bias, robustness and security testing on your own data and threat model.
6. **Approval:** risk tier, conditions and owner (Module 3.5), with an inventory and AIBOM entry.
7. **Operation:** pinned version, monitoring, re-testing after changes, and an exit plan.

blocks.title: Foundation model questions
blocks.md: Remember three ideas. **Accountability stays with you**: using a vendor’s model doesn’t transfer responsibility for your system. **Every change is a new model**: fine-tunes and version upgrades need re-evaluation. **Testing can’t prove the absence of backdoors**, so combine trusted provenance, testing, least privilege and monitoring.

blocks.title: The quiet upgrade
blocks.md: A retailer’s returns assistant calls a hosted foundation model through the provider’s “latest” alias. One Monday, replies start arriving in a slightly different format, a downstream parser fails, and testers notice the assistant now agrees to requests it used to refuse. The provider had released a new model version over the weekend and moved the alias to it.

q.q: Which control would MOST likely have prevented this disruption?
o: Asking the provider to email the team whenever it plans to release a new model
Pinning a dated model version, and re-testing before moving to any new one
Switching to a different provider whose releases are usually less frequent
Adding more examples to the system prompt to make the reply format stricter
q.why: Pinning stops the provider changing the model underneath the application, and re-testing before an upgrade catches format and safety changes. Emails and release frequency don’t give control, and prompt tweaks don’t address the safety change.

q.q: A team fine-tunes an approved open-weight model on 2,000 internal support tickets. The base model passed the organisation’s safety evaluations last quarter. What should happen before the fine-tuned model is deployed?
o: Nothing further, because the base model already passed the organisation’s safety evaluations
Re-run safety and security evaluations on the fine-tuned model, and approve it as a new version
Ask the base model’s publisher to confirm that fine-tuning won’t have changed its behaviour
Deploy it to all users at once, and check customer complaints for safety problems afterwards
q.why: Fine-tuning can weaken safety behaviour, even on benign data, so the fine-tuned model is a new model that needs its own evaluation and approval. The publisher can’t vouch for your fine-tune, and relying on complaints means users find the problems first.

quiz.q: Why is a dataset distributed as a list of URLs especially exposed to poisoning?
o: URL lists are too large to store, so they are rarely backed up anywhere
The content behind each URL can change after curation, including on expired domains
URL lists can only be downloaded over unencrypted connections, never over TLS
Search engines index URL lists, which reveals the dataset’s full contents to attackers
quiz.why: Whoever controls a URL controls what later downloaders receive. Hashes recorded at curation time let users reject changed content.

quiz.q: Which control MOST directly ensures that a model is trained on exactly the data that was reviewed?
o: Downloading the dataset again at the start of every training run
Pinning each item by content hash in an internal, access-controlled mirror
Choosing the datasets with the most downloads on the public hub
Asking data scientists to record the exact date they downloaded each dataset
quiz.why: Content hashes and a controlled mirror fix the training data and make any change detectable. Live downloads, popularity and dates don’t.

quiz.q: A purchased dataset of consumer profiles is offered for model training. Which question is MOST important to answer first?
o: How many columns the dataset contains, and which file format it uses
How the data was collected, and whether there is a lawful basis for training
Whether the vendor can deliver the data faster than its competitors can
Whether other companies in the same sector have already used the dataset
quiz.why: Personal data collected without a lawful basis, or permission for this use, creates legal risk that no technical control fixes later.

quiz.q: Why is synthetic data generated by another model not automatically low-risk?
o: Synthetic data is always much larger than the real data it replaces
It can inherit the generator’s biases and errors, and carry its licence terms
Regulators prohibit training models on any data that other AI models have generated
Synthetic data can’t be stored in the same systems as real customer data
quiz.why: Synthetic data reflects the model that made it, including its flaws, and the generating model’s terms may restrict how outputs are used.

quiz.q: What does a valid digital signature on a model file prove?
o: That the model contains no backdoors or known vulnerabilities
That the holder of the key or identity signed it, and it hasn’t changed since
That the model performs as well as its model card claims it does on every benchmark
That the model’s licence permits your intended commercial use
quiz.why: Signatures prove origin and integrity, not safety or quality. A compromised publisher can still sign a malicious release.

o: Two internal teams deploying the same model under different names
Re-registering a deleted publisher’s name, so name-based references pull an impostor
Fine-tuning a public model and then republishing it under the original publisher’s name
Reusing a model’s tokenizer with a completely different set of weights
quiz.why: Pipelines that reference models by publisher and name trust whoever holds that name. Pinning by hash and internal mirrors prevent substitution.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST prevents dependency confusion attacks on internal ML packages?
o: Automatically installing the newest available version of every package, every time
Private indexes with scoped names, so internal names can’t resolve publicly
Asking developers to check package names carefully before installing
Allowing package installation only during normal business hours
quiz.why: Dependency confusion relies on installers preferring a public package with an internal name. Scoped private indexes and pinned sources remove that path.

quiz.q: Which evidence shows HOW a third-party model artefact was built?
o: A marketing brochure that describes the model’s capabilities in detail
A signed provenance attestation describing the source, inputs and pipeline
A list of well-known customers that already use the model in production
A screenshot of the model’s download page on a popular public hub
quiz.why: Provenance attestations record how an artefact was produced, and their signatures let you check that they match the artefact you received.

quiz.q: Why should a fine-tuned model be re-evaluated for safety, even if its base model passed?
o: Fine-tuning always reduces a model’s accuracy on its main task
Fine-tuning, even on a small amount of data, can weaken safety behaviour
Regulators require a new licence for every fine-tuned model version
Fine-tuned models can’t be stored in the same model registry as their base models
quiz.why: Research shows that fine-tuning can erode safety training, sometimes with very few examples, so every fine-tune is a new model to evaluate.

quiz.q: Which statement about backdoors in pre-trained models is MOST accurate?
o: Standard safety training reliably removes any backdoor that a pre-trained model contains
Testing can’t rule out hidden triggers, so provenance and monitoring matter too
Backdoors exist only in models that are distributed in pickle format
Backdoors can always be found by reading the model card carefully
quiz.why: Backdoors can survive safety training and evade testing, so trusted provenance, least privilege and production monitoring complement evaluation.

quiz.q: What is the MAIN risk of calling a hosted foundation model through an unpinned alias such as “latest”?
o: The provider may charge more for calls made through an alias
The model behind the alias can change without your testing or approval
Aliases always point to older, deprecated versions of the model
Calls made through aliases bypass the provider’s safety systems and content filters
quiz.why: An alias lets the provider swap the underlying model. Pin dated versions, and re-test before moving to a new one.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of general-purpose AI models give downstream providers?
o: Full copies of their training data, whenever a downstream provider asks
Information and documentation on the model’s capabilities and limitations
A guarantee that the model will never produce incorrect or harmful output
Exclusive rights to use the model within the downstream provider’s sector
quiz.why: Article 53 requires general-purpose AI model providers to give downstream providers the information they need to understand the model and meet their own obligations.

exam.q: A healthcare start-up wants to fine-tune a diagnostic model on a large open medical imaging dataset found on a public hub. The dataset page has no licence, no datasheet and an anonymous uploader. What should the security and privacy lead recommend?
o: Use it, because publicly available data can be used freely for both research and products
Don’t use it until provenance, licence, consent and content are established; find a documented source
Use it only for internal testing, which removes the legal and privacy obligations that would apply
Use a random 10% sample, which reduces the legal exposure and the poisoning risk proportionately
exam.why: Medical images are special category data, and an undocumented, unlicensed dataset from an anonymous source fails provenance, rights and lawful-basis checks. Public availability doesn’t grant rights, internal use is still processing, and sampling doesn’t fix legality or poisoning.

exam.q: An AI team learns that a public dataset it trained on six months ago has been withdrawn after illegal content was found in it. What should happen FIRST?
o: Nothing, because the models were trained before the dataset was withdrawn
Assess exposure: identify affected models and data copies, and involve legal and compliance
Delete every model in production immediately, whatever the impact on the business
Publish a statement saying the organisation wasn’t aware of the content when it trained the models
exam.why: Lineage and the AIBOM let the team find every affected copy and model; legal and compliance decide on obligations such as deletion, reporting and retraining. Doing nothing ignores the risk, mass deletion is premature, and statements come after the facts are known.

exam.q: A vendor delivers a fine-tuned model signed with its own key, but with no provenance attestation or model card. The vendor says the model “passed all internal tests”. What is the BEST next step?
o: Accept it, because the valid signature shows that the model is safe to deploy
Request provenance and documentation, and test the model independently in a sandbox
Reject the vendor permanently, because missing documents prove the model is malicious
Deploy it to a small group of customers, and gather their feedback before deciding
exam.why: A signature proves origin, not safety. Documentation and provenance support the assessment, and independent testing in isolation verifies the vendor’s claims before approval. Permanent rejection is disproportionate, and customer pilots expose users to an unverified model.

exam.q: A popular model-loading library was briefly replaced on the public package registry by a malicious version. An organisation’s builds install the latest version automatically. Which control would MOST have reduced its exposure?
o: A policy requiring developers to read the library’s changelog every month before each release
Dependencies pinned by version and hash, installed from a verified internal mirror
Running builds less often, so that fewer malicious versions get installed
Switching to a different library that has fewer outside contributors
exam.why: Pinned, hash-verified dependencies from an internal mirror don’t change when the public registry does. Changelogs, build frequency and contributor counts don’t stop a malicious version being installed.

exam.q: A bank plans to use a hosted foundation model to triage customer complaints, a process with regulatory deadlines. Which combination BEST manages the foundation model risk?
o: Rely on the provider’s strong reputation and on its standard terms of service
Pin the version, evaluate on the bank’s data, agree change notice, and keep a fallback
Adopt each new model version as soon as it is released, to get the best accuracy
Ask staff to double-check every triage decision, so that no other controls are needed
exam.why: Pinning prevents silent changes, the bank’s own evaluation tests fitness for its use, contractual notice gives time to re-test, and a fallback protects the deadline. Reputation isn’t a control, chasing versions skips testing, and manual checks alone don’t address availability or change.

exam.q: A product team wants to build on an open-weight model whose licence restricts use by companies above a set number of monthly active users. The product is expected to pass that threshold within a year. What should happen?
o: Proceed, because the licence terms of open-weight models can’t be enforced
Have legal review the licence first, and pick a model or agreement that fits the scale
Proceed now, and negotiate a commercial licence only if the model provider complains later
Remove the model’s attribution notices, so that the licence no longer applies to it
exam.why: Licence terms are part of the supply chain risk assessment. Legal review before adoption avoids building on a model the product will soon be barred from using. Ignoring or evading terms creates legal exposure.
